blogs.title: Ciminelli Did Not Kill the Pump-and-Dump Case: The Fifth Circuit’s Property Theory in Constantinescu
blogs.description: This post would examine the opinion’s central doctrinal move: distinguishing the forbidden right-to-control theory from a permissible fraudulent-inducement theory. It would explain why the Fifth Circuit treated the followers’ trading dollars—not merely their lost access to accurate information—as the property interest at stake, and why that matters for fraud prosecutions after the Supreme Court’s recent narrowing decisions.

blogs.title: Profit Without Proving Loss: How Constantinescu Imports Kousisis into Securities Fraud
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s treatment of intent to defraud and its rejection of the defendants’ argument that they only meant to profit, not to harm. The key question is whether criminal fraud requires intended net economic loss; Constantinescu answers no, using Kousisis to suggest that the fraud is complete once money or property is obtained through material deception, even if the victim receives market-value securities in return.

blogs.title: Section 1348 as Mail-and-Wire Fraud’s Securities Cousin
blogs.description: This post would explore the court’s methodology in construing 18 U.S.C. § 1348 through analogies to mail and wire fraud doctrine. Because Fifth Circuit precedent on § 1348 remains thin, Constantinescu is significant for showing how general fraud concepts—scheme to defraud, intent, property, and indictment sufficiency—are being imported into criminal securities cases, potentially broadening DOJ’s charging flexibility.

blogs.title: From Finfluencer Hype to Federal Fraud: What Constantinescu Means for Social-Media Market Manipulation
blogs.description: This post would place the case in the broader trend of applying traditional fraud statutes to online investing communities and social-media stock promotion. It would consider the line the opinion draws between actionable deception—especially lies about one’s own trading position and undisclosed dumping—and ordinary bullish talk, as well as the practical implications for traders, influencers, prosecutors, and defense counsel on remand.
